content.text: White House's historic FY-27 defense budget fueled by $350B reconciliation request The White House Office of Management and Budget is preparing to send Congress a $1.5 trillion fiscal year 2027 defense budget request that relies on $350 billion in mandatory funding outside the traditional appropriations process, aiming for about $760 billion in total weapons procurement and modernization, according to officials who described the plan to Inside Defense ahead of its release. OMB officials said the Trump administration’s base FY-27 discretionary defense request will be $1.15 trillion, accompanied by a request for $350 billion in mandatory defense spending under a second budget reconciliation bill. The Pentagon’s base FY-27 procurement account will be just under $260 billion, while the base request for research, development, test and evaluation will be just under $220 billion. Through a new reconciliation package, the department will seek another $280 billion for procurement and RDT&E, bringing the Pentagon’s total requested “modernization account” to around $760 billion. The “overall theme” of the budget, one official said, is “really shifting from a sustainment-based force to a force that is investing in productive expansion of the industrial base and delivery of new innovation.” Nearly all of the $17.5 billion being sought for the Golden Dome missile defense system will be in the reconciliation request, with around $400 million in the base request. Significant new investment in shipbuilding will be a key feature of both requests as DOD seeks $65.8 billion to procure 18 battle force ships and 16 non-battle force vessels as part of a broader push -- across recent budget submissions and related legislation -- that the administration says would fund 123 ships. Officials cast the funding as a sustained effort to rebuild U.S. shipbuilding capacity and expand the fleet, noting that the administration wants to expand shipbuilding beyond traditional prime contractors to drive more competition into the sector and increase production capacity. Officials said the F-35 Joint Strike Fighter is also poised for a “major shift” upward in procurement as promising new capabilities with Block 4 upgrades have started to come online. The total number of F-35s requested for FY-27 will be 85, with 32 of them funded via the base budget and 53 funded via mandatory spending in reconciliation. The budget seeks 38 F-35As, 10 F-35Bs, and 37 F-35Cs. In contrast, the department sought to purchase only 47 total F-35s in FY-26. Officials also said the budget will continue to seek robust funding for the F-47 Next Generation Air Dominance platform. A significant share of the proposed funding increase will also be directed toward rebuilding industrial capacity and addressing munitions shortfalls, areas the administration has identified as critical in light of sustained global demand and the potential for future high-end conflicts. OMB officials said the FY-27 request will fund all of the Pentagon’s critical munitions “framework” deals announced in the past few months that have been focused on expanding industry’s production capacity -- and getting the private sector to invest more of its own capital to do so. “You’ll see an investment there that is really focused not just on building up our inventory of these critical munitions but expanding the munitions industrial base,” an official said. The budget also includes targeted investments in drones, critical mineral supply chains and emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence and autonomous systems. Beyond modernization, the budget includes provisions aimed at improving quality of life and readiness across the force. The plan proposes tiered military pay raises ranging from 5% to 7% along with additional investments in barracks and facility sustainment. Medical readiness funding includes support for trauma care systems, staffing at casualty-receiving facilities and expanded virtual health capabilities. Officials said a future years defense program will be made available but did not detail how much of the elevated funding level would persist beyond FY-27, leaving open questions about whether the proposal represents a permanent shift in the defense spending baseline. Where a historic request meets politics If the White House can bring the final FY-27 topline to $1.5 trillion, it will represent a 44% increase, exceeding the Reagan buildup and approaching levels not seen since World War II. But the structure of the request could complicate its reception on Capitol Hill, where some GOP lawmakers, noting their razor-thin majority in the House, have voiced opposition to boosting defense spending using a second reconciliation bill. How congressional Republicans respond -- particularly whether they embrace the use of mandatory funding or seek to fold those resources back into the base budget -- is likely to shape the trajectory of defense spending in the years ahead. OMB officials said the push for a second reconciliation bill comes from the success the White House saw with the OBBA and the strategic desire to avoid a spending negotiation with Democrats, who will likely seek to increase non-defense funds in exchange for their support for additional defense spending. OMB Director Russ Vought previewed the approach at a defense conference in December, noting the OBBA was a “paradigm shift” for beating Democratic opposition in the Senate, where the filibuster remains intact. Senior Republicans said last week they are ready to pursue a second reconciliation bill, but House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) noted at the time it would be far from easy. Additionally, Congress is anticipating a supplemental defense spending request related to the ongoing U.S. military campaign in Iran. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth confirmed that the Pentagon sent OMB a $200 billion request but stressed that the number could change. While OMB is scheduled to release more detailed information tomorrow, the Pentagon is slated to hold its own budget rollout on April 21, supported by additional justification documents and public briefings.
